anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: How do you distinguish an UMN from an LMN facial (CN VII) palsy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: LMN (Bell’s palsy) weakens the whole ipsilateral face, including the forehead; UMN (stroke) spares the forehead (the upper face has bilateral cortical input).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Besides facial movement, what else does the facial nerve carry?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Taste (anterior ⅔ of the tongue, via the chorda tympani), motor to stapedius (loss → hyperacusis), and parasympathetic lacrimation & salivation.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Name the five branches of the facial nerve.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical (“Two Zebras Bit My Coat”).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the features of a thyroglossal cyst?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: A midline neck cyst (at/below the hyoid) that moves up on swallowing AND tongue protrusion (tethered to the foramen caecum by its tract).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: How does a thyroid mass differ from a thyroglossal cyst on examination?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: A thyroid mass moves up on swallowing but NOT on tongue protrusion (it has no lingual attachment).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: What is a branchial cyst?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: A lateral neck cyst at the anterior border of the upper ⅓ of sternocleidomastoid (a 2nd branchial cleft remnant), typically in young adults.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Which nerve is at risk in thyroid surgery near the inferior thyroid artery, and what is the consequence?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (in the tracheo-oesophageal groove) → a hoarse voice / vocal cord palsy; bilateral injury → airway obstruction (may need tracheostomy).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Which nerve is at risk near the superior thyroid artery, and its effect?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve → weakness of cricothyroid → a weak, easily-tired voice (can’t reach high notes).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: What complication follows inadvertent parathyroid removal?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Hypocalcaemia — perioral tingling, Chvostek’s & Trousseau’s signs and tetany.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the relationship of the facial nerve to the parotid gland?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The facial nerve (CN VII) passes through the parotid, dividing it into superficial & deep lobes — so a parotid tumour or surgery can cause a facial palsy (though CN VII does not supply the gland).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the secretomotor supply of the parotid gland?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) — its parasympathetic fibres relay in the otic ganglion.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Where does the parotid (Stensen's) duct open?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Into the mouth opposite the 2nd upper molar.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Which salivary gland is the commonest site of stones, and why?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The submandibular gland (via Wharton’s duct) — its saliva is more viscous/mucous and the duct runs uphill; a stone → painful swelling at mealtimes.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Through what structure is an emergency cricothyroidotomy performed?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The cricothyroid membrane (between the thyroid & cricoid cartilages) — superficial and relatively avascular.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Through which tracheal rings is a tracheostomy performed?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The 2nd–4th tracheal rings — the thyroid isthmus overlies these rings and is usually divided or retracted.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Which laryngeal cartilage is the only complete ring, and its clinical use?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The cricoid cartilage — used for cricoid pressure during rapid-sequence induction.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: List the five layers of the scalp (SCALP).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Skin, dense Connective tissue, Aponeurosis (epicranius), Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Why do scalp wounds bleed profusely?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The arteries in the dense connective tissue layer are held open (they cannot retract), so lacerations bleed heavily.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Why is the loose areolar layer of the scalp the 'dangerous area'?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Infection spreads easily within it and can reach the intracranial venous sinuses via emissary veins → meningitis/venous sinus thrombosis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Describe an extradural haematoma.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Arterial bleeding, usually from the middle meningeal artery at the pterion (thin bone); a lucid interval then deterioration; a biconvex (lens) shape on CT.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Describe a subdural haematoma.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Venous bleeding from torn bridging veins (elderly, alcoholics, shaken babies); a crescent (concave) shape; often slower onset.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the pterion, and why is it clinically important?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The H-shaped junction of the frontal, parietal, temporal & sphenoid bones — the thinnest part of the skull, overlying the middle meningeal artery (fracture → extradural haematoma).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the features of a CN III (oculomotor) palsy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: A “down & out” eye, ptosis and (in a surgical/compressive cause) a fixed dilated pupil — e.g. a posterior communicating artery aneurysm or uncal herniation.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: What is Horner's syndrome, and two causes?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Ptosis, miosis & anhidrosis from disruption of the sympathetic supply to the head — e.g. a Pancoast tumour or carotid dissection.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Which structures run through the cavernous sinus?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 & VI and the internal carotid artery (VI & the carotid lie within it; III, IV, V1, V2 in its lateral wall).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: How can a facial infection cause cavernous sinus thrombosis?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: Via the valveless facial → ophthalmic veins draining into the cavernous sinus (the “danger triangle” of the face).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: At what level does the common carotid artery bifurcate, and into what?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: At about C4 (the upper border of the thyroid cartilage), into the internal & external carotid arteries.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the carotid sinus and carotid body?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: At the bifurcation: the carotid sinus is a baroreceptor (CN IX) and the carotid body is a chemoreceptor (O₂/CO₂/pH).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.front: Which vein is targeted for central venous access in the neck?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.back: The internal jugular vein (lateral to the common carotid, deep to sternocleidomastoid).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What are the two functional divisions of the skull, and how many bones each?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The neurocranium (8 bones) enclosing the brain, and the viscerocranium/facial skeleton (14 bones).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: Name the eight bones of the neurocranium.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Frontal, 2 parietal, 2 temporal, occipital, sphenoid & ethmoid.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What is the structure of the calvaria (skull cap)?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: A sandwich of an outer table, diploë (spongy bone with marrow & diploic veins) and an inner table.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: Name the major cranial sutures.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The coronal (frontal–parietal), sagittal (between the parietals), lambdoid (parietal–occipital) and squamous sutures.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What is the pterion, and why is it important?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The H-shaped junction of the frontal, parietal, temporal & sphenoid bones — the thinnest part of the skull, overlying the middle meningeal artery (fracture → extradural haematoma).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: Define bregma and lambda.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Bregma = junction of the coronal & sagittal sutures; lambda = junction of the sagittal & lambdoid sutures.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: When do the anterior and posterior fontanelles close?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The anterior fontanelle (at the bregma) closes at ~18 months; the posterior fontanelle (at the lambda) closes at ~2–3 months.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: How is the anterior fontanelle used clinically?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: A bulging fontanelle suggests raised ICP/meningitis; a sunken fontanelle suggests dehydration.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What is craniosynostosis?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Premature fusion of a cranial suture, producing an abnormal head shape (e.g. sagittal fusion → a long, narrow scaphocephaly).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What does the anterior cranial fossa contain and transmit?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The frontal lobes; the cribriform plate of the ethmoid transmits the olfactory nerve (CN I).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What are the key features of the middle cranial fossa?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: It holds the temporal lobes and the sella turcica (pituitary), and contains most of the skull-base foramina.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What does the posterior cranial fossa contain?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The brainstem & cerebellum, with the foramen magnum transmitting the medulla/cord and vertebral arteries.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What passes through the optic canal?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What passes through the superior orbital fissure?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Cranial nerves III, IV, V1 & VI and the ophthalmic veins.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What passes through the foramen rotundum and the foramen ovale?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Rotundum → CN V2 (maxillary); ovale → CN V3 (mandibular).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What passes through the foramen spinosum?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The middle meningeal artery (and the meningeal branch of V3).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What passes through the internal acoustic meatus?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Cranial nerves VII (facial) & VIII (vestibulocochlear) and the labyrinthine artery.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What passes through the jugular foramen?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Cranial nerves IX, X & XI and the internal jugular vein / sigmoid sinus.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What passes through the hypoglossal canal?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: Through which foramen does the facial nerve exit the skull?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The stylomastoid foramen.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What passes through the foramen magnum?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The medulla/spinal cord, the vertebral arteries, the spinal root of CN XI and the meninges.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: Describe the parts of the mandible.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: A body (with the tooth-bearing alveolar part) and two rami; each ramus has a condylar & a coronoid process, meeting the body at the angle.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What do the mandibular and mental foramina transmit?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The mandibular foramen admits the inferior alveolar nerve (dental block); the mental foramen transmits the mental nerve.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: Classify the temporomandibular joint and give its movements.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: A synovial joint with an articular disc; it allows elevation/depression, protrusion/retrusion and side-to-side movement (depression begins with lateral pterygoid).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What happens in anterior TMJ dislocation?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The mandibular condyle passes anterior to the articular tubercle (e.g. a wide yawn), locking the mouth open.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: How many bones form the orbit, and what is at its apex?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Seven bones (frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxilla, ethmoid, lacrimal, palatine); the optic canal is at the apex.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What is an orbital blowout fracture?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Fracture of a thin orbital wall: the floor (maxilla) — commonest — can trap the inferior rectus → diplopia on upgaze; a medial wall (ethmoid) fracture may instead trap the medial rectus (horizontal diplopia).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: Name the paranasal sinuses.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: The frontal, maxillary, ethmoidal & sphenoidal sinuses (air-filled, draining into the nasal meatuses).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.front: What are the signs of a base-of-skull fracture?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.back: Raccoon eyes (periorbital bruising), Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising), CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea and haemotympanum.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: From which pharyngeal arch do the muscles of facial expression develop, and what supplies them?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The 2nd pharyngeal arch; they are all supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Where do the muscles of facial expression insert, and what is special about their covering?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: Most insert into the skin (so they move the skin, not bone), and there is no investing deep fascia over them.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What is the action of orbicularis oculi, and the consequence of its paralysis?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: It closes the eye (palpebral part = blinking, orbital part = forced closure); paralysis → inability to close the eye → corneal exposure/drying.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What are the actions of buccinator, and which nerve supplies it?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: It compresses the cheek to keep food on the teeth (and aids blowing); supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII) — it is a muscle of facial expression, NOT of mastication; the parotid duct pierces it.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What joins the two bellies of occipitofrontalis?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurosis); the muscle raises the eyebrows & wrinkles the forehead.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What is the action of orbicularis oris?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: It closes and purses the lips (essential for speech & whistling).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Describe the intracranial course of the facial nerve.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: It enters the internal acoustic meatus, runs in the facial canal (at the geniculate ganglion), and exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What does the facial nerve do after leaving the stylomastoid foramen?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: It supplies posterior belly of digastric, stylohyoid & the posterior auricular muscle, then enters the parotid gland and divides into its five terminal branches.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Name the five terminal branches of the facial nerve.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular & Cervical (“Two Zebras Bit My Coat”).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: List the four functional components of the facial nerve.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: Motor (facial expression + stapedius, posterior digastric, stylohyoid); taste (anterior ⅔ tongue via chorda tympani); parasympathetic (lacrimal, submandibular & sublingual glands); and a little general sensory.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What are the three intracranial branches of the facial nerve, and their functions?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The greater petrosal nerve (→ lacrimal & nasal glands), the nerve to stapedius (dampens loud sound), and the chorda tympani (taste ant ⅔ tongue + submandibular/sublingual glands).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Which nerve provides GENERAL sensation to the face?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The trigeminal nerve (CN V), via its three divisions (V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, V3 mandibular).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Give the sensory territory of V1 (ophthalmic).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The forehead, upper eyelid, dorsum of the nose and the cornea (exits via the superior orbital fissure).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Give the sensory territory of V2 (maxillary).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip and side of the nose (exits via the foramen rotundum).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Give the sensory territory of V3 (mandibular).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The lower lip, chin, jaw and general sensation of the anterior ⅔ of the tongue (exits via the foramen ovale); it also carries motor to the muscles of mastication.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What supplies the skin over the ANGLE of the jaw (not the trigeminal)?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) — so the angle of the jaw is spared in a trigeminal (V3) lesion.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: List the five layers of the scalp (SCALP).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: Skin, dense Connective tissue, Aponeurosis (galea/epicranius), Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Which three scalp layers move together as a unit?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The skin, connective tissue & aponeurosis (bound together); they glide on the loose areolar layer.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Where do the scalp arteries run, and what is their origin?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: In the dense connective-tissue layer; from the external carotid (superficial temporal, posterior auricular, occipital) and the ophthalmic/ICA (supratrochlear, supraorbital) — with rich anastomoses across the midline.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Why do scalp wounds bleed profusely?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: The arteries are held open by the dense connective tissue (cannot retract) and anastomose freely, so lacerations bleed heavily.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Give the nerve supply of the anterior and posterior scalp.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: Anterior — trigeminal (supratrochlear/supraorbital V1, zygomaticotemporal V2, auriculotemporal V3); posterior — cervical nerves (greater occipital C2, lesser occipital C2–C3, third occipital C3).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Describe the course of the facial artery, and where its pulse is felt.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: A branch of the external carotid; it crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the anterior edge of masseter (palpable pulse) and runs tortuously to the medial canthus as the angular artery.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Why is the facial vein clinically dangerous?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: It is valveless and connects (via the ophthalmic veins & pterygoid plexus) to the cavernous sinus — so infection in the danger triangle can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: Where is the 'danger triangle' of the face?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: From the bridge of the nose to the corners of the mouth — infection here can spread to the cavernous sinus via the valveless facial vein.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What are the features of a Bell's (LMN) facial palsy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: Weakness of the whole ipsilateral face, including the forehead, ± dry eye, hyperacusis and loss of taste (depending on the level of the lesion).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: How does an UMN facial lesion (stroke) differ from an LMN one?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: An UMN lesion spares the forehead (bilateral cortical input to the upper facial muscles); an LMN lesion involves the whole face.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What are the afferent and efferent limbs of the corneal (blink) reflex?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: Afferent = V1 (nasociliary/ophthalmic); efferent = CN VII (orbicularis oculi).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What is trigeminal neuralgia?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: Paroxysmal, severe, lancinating facial pain (usually in the V2/V3 territory), triggered by light touch, chewing or cold.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.front: What is Hutchinson's sign in herpes zoster ophthalmicus?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.back: Vesicles on the tip of the nose — indicating nasociliary nerve (V1) involvement, which warns of ocular/corneal disease.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Name the four layers of the deep cervical fascia.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The investing, pretracheal, prevertebral layers and the carotid sheath.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What does the investing layer of deep cervical fascia enclose?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: It surrounds the whole neck and splits to enclose sternocleidomastoid & trapezius (and the parotid & submandibular glands).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What does the pretracheal fascia enclose?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The thyroid gland, trachea & oesophagus (and the infrahyoid strap muscles).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What lies within the prevertebral fascia, and what does it become laterally?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The vertebral column & deep (prevertebral/scalene) muscles; it extends laterally as the axillary sheath around the brachial plexus.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Why are the cervical fascial spaces clinically important?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: They form potential spaces (retropharyngeal / “danger” space) that can channel infection down into the mediastinum.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What are the boundaries of the anterior triangle of the neck?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The midline of the neck, the inferior border of the mandible & the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Name the four subdivisions of the anterior triangle.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The submental, submandibular (digastric), carotid & muscular triangles.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What are the boundaries of the posterior triangle?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The posterior border of SCM, the anterior border of trapezius & the middle third of the clavicle.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: List the main contents of the posterior triangle.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The accessory nerve (CN XI), the cervical plexus branches, the trunks of the brachial plexus, the 3rd part of the subclavian artery, the external jugular vein & the inferior belly of omohyoid.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Why is the accessory nerve vulnerable in the posterior triangle?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: It runs superficially (only under investing fascia), so it is easily injured during lymph-node biopsy → trapezius weakness & a drooping shoulder.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Describe the attachments and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: From sternal & clavicular heads to the mastoid process & superior nuchal line; supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI) (+ C2–3 proprioception).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What are the actions of sternocleidomastoid?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: Unilaterally it tilts the head to the same side and rotates the face to the opposite side; bilaterally it flexes the neck (congenital shortening → torticollis).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Name the infrahyoid (strap) muscles and their general action.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: Sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid & omohyoid — they depress the hyoid/larynx.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What is the nerve supply of the infrahyoid muscles?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The ansa cervicalis (C1–C3) — except thyrohyoid, which is supplied by C1 alone (travelling with the hypoglossal nerve).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Name the suprahyoid muscles.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: Digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid & geniohyoid — they elevate the hyoid.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: From which roots is the cervical plexus formed, and where does it lie?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: From the anterior rami of C1–C4, deep to sternocleidomastoid.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Name the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical & supraclavicular nerves.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Where do the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: At the nerve point of the neck (Erb’s point) — the middle of the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What are the two main motor branches of the cervical plexus?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The ansa cervicalis (C1–C3) (to the strap muscles) and the phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What are the roots and function of the phrenic nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: C3, C4 & C5 (“keep the diaphragm alive”); it is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm and descends on scalenus anterior.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What are the contents of the carotid sheath?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The common/internal carotid artery (medial), the internal jugular vein (lateral) & the vagus nerve (posterior, between them).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: At what level does the common carotid bifurcate, and what sits there?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: At ~C4 (upper border of the thyroid cartilage); the carotid sinus (baroreceptor) & carotid body (chemoreceptor) lie at the bifurcation.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: How is the subclavian artery divided in the root of the neck?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: Into three parts relative to scalenus anterior (1st medial, 2nd posterior, 3rd lateral); it arches over the 1st rib.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What passes through the interscalene triangle?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The trunks of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery (between scalenus anterior & medius) — the site of thoracic outlet compression.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: On which side does the thoracic duct drain at the root of the neck?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The left — it arches over to drain into the left venous angle (junction of the left internal jugular & subclavian veins).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What is Ludwig's angina?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: Cellulitis of the submandibular / floor-of-mouth space (often dental) that can spread and obstruct the airway.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: What is a retropharyngeal abscess, and why is it dangerous?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: An infection in the retropharyngeal space; it can track down the fascial “danger space” into the mediastinum (mediastinitis).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.front: Where is central venous access in the neck usually obtained?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.back: The internal jugular vein (within the carotid sheath, lateral to the common carotid).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Name the four extrinsic muscles of the tongue and their actions.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Genioglossus (protrudes), Hyoglossus (depresses), Styloglossus (retracts/elevates), Palatoglossus (elevates the posterior tongue).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What is the motor supply of the tongue muscles, and the exception?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: All are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) — EXCEPT palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Give the sensory (general & taste) supply of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: General sensation = the lingual nerve (V3); taste = the chorda tympani (CN VII).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Give the sensory supply of the posterior third of the tongue.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Both general sensation and taste = the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: In a hypoglossal (CN XII) palsy, which way does the tongue deviate on protrusion, and why?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: It deviates toward the side of the lesion — the paralysed genioglossus cannot push that side forward (“the tongue points to the lesion”).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Name the three parts of the pharynx.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: The nasopharynx, oropharynx & laryngopharynx.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Name the muscles of the pharyngeal wall.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Three circular constrictors (superior, middle, inferior) and three longitudinal muscles (stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What is the motor and sensory supply of the pharynx (and the exception)?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Motor = the pharyngeal plexus (CN X) for all EXCEPT stylopharyngeus (CN IX); sensory is mainly CN IX.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What is Waldeyer's ring?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: The ring of lymphoid tissue in the pharynx: the pharyngeal (adenoid), tubal, palatine & lingual tonsils.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What is a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum)?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: A mucosal herniation through Killian’s dehiscence (a weak point between the thyropharyngeus & cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor) → dysphagia, regurgitation & halitosis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Name the main laryngeal cartilages.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: The thyroid, cricoid (the only complete ring), the paired arytenoids and the epiglottis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What is the nerve supply of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles, and the exception?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: All are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve — EXCEPT the cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Which laryngeal muscle is the only abductor of the vocal cords?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: The posterior cricoarytenoid — it “opens” the cords and is vital for breathing (“PCA opens”).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What supplies sensation above and below the vocal cords?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Above the cords = the internal laryngeal nerve (from the superior laryngeal); below = the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What happens with unilateral and bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Unilateral → hoarseness (a cord fixed in the paramedian position); bilateral → airway obstruction (both posterior cricoarytenoids paralysed).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Name the three ossicles of the middle ear.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: The malleus, incus & stapes.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What does the Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube connect, and its function?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: It connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure across the tympanic membrane.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Why is otitis media common in young children?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Their Eustachian tube is shorter, wider & more horizontal, so nasopharyngeal infection ascends easily to the middle ear.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What does the inner ear contain?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: The cochlea (hearing) and the vestibular apparatus (balance), supplied by the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Distinguish conductive from sensorineural hearing loss.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Conductive = a problem in the external/middle ear (sound conduction); sensorineural = a problem in the cochlea or CN VIII — separated clinically by the Rinne & Weber tests.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Name the six extraocular muscles.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Four recti (superior, inferior, medial, lateral) and two obliques (superior & inferior).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Give the cranial nerve supply of the extraocular muscles (LR6 SO4 rest 3).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Lateral rectus = CN VI (abducens), superior oblique = CN IV (trochlear), and all the rest = CN III (oculomotor).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What are the afferent and efferent limbs of the pupillary light reflex?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Afferent = CN II (optic); efferent = CN III (oculomotor) (parasympathetic to the sphincter pupillae).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What are the features of a CN III (oculomotor) palsy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: A “down & out” eye, ptosis and a dilated pupil (if the parasympathetic fibres are involved).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What deficit results from a CN IV (trochlear) palsy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Vertical diplopia (worse looking down & in, e.g. going downstairs) with a compensatory head tilt away from the affected side (weak superior oblique).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What deficit results from a CN VI (abducens) palsy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: Failure to abduct the eye → horizontal diplopia (weak lateral rectus).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: What is quinsy, and the tonsil's main blood supply?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: A peritonsillar abscess (a complication of tonsillitis); the palatine tonsil is supplied chiefly by the tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.front: Which nerve supplies BOTH taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, and is at risk in tonsillectomy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.back: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Give the mnemonic for the names of the cranial nerves in order.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: “On Old Olympus’ Towering Tops A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops” — Olfactory, Optic, Oculomotor, Trochlear, Trigeminal, Abducens, Facial, vestibulocochlear (Auditory), Glossopharyngeal, Vagus, Spinal accessory, Hypoglossal.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which cranial nerves are purely SENSORY?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: I (olfactory), II (optic) & VIII (vestibulocochlear) — the “S”s in “Some Say Marry Money…”

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which cranial nerves are MIXED (both sensory and motor)?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: V (trigeminal), VII (facial), IX (glossopharyngeal) & X (vagus).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which four cranial nerves carry PARASYMPATHETIC fibres?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: III, VII, IX & X — relaying in the ciliary (III), pterygopalatine & submandibular (VII), otic (IX) ganglia, and the visceral walls (X).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Through which skull opening does CN I pass?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Through which opening does the optic nerve (II) pass?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: The optic canal (with the ophthalmic artery).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which cranial nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: III, IV, V1 & VI.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Through which foramina do the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve exit?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: V1 — superior orbital fissure; V2 — foramen rotundum; V3 — foramen ovale.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which cranial nerves pass through the internal acoustic meatus?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: VII (facial) & VIII (vestibulocochlear) — VII then exits the skull via the stylomastoid foramen.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which cranial nerves pass through the jugular foramen?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: IX, X & XI (with the internal jugular vein).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Through which canal does the hypoglossal nerve (XII) exit?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: The hypoglossal canal.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which cranial nerve nuclei lie in the MIDBRAIN?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: III (oculomotor) & IV (trochlear).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which cranial nerve nuclei lie in the PONS?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: V, VI, VII & VIII.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which cranial nerve nuclei lie in the MEDULLA?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: IX, X, XII (and the cranial part of XI); the spinal accessory arises from the upper cervical cord (C1–C5).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: What is special about the trochlear nerve (IV)?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: It is the only cranial nerve to exit the DORSAL brainstem and it decussates (supplies the contralateral superior oblique); it is also the thinnest.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Why does the abducens nerve (VI) act as a 'false localising sign'?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: It has a long intracranial course with a sharp bend over the petrous apex (Dorello’s canal), so it is stretched by raised intracranial pressure, causing a palsy that does not reflect the site of the lesion.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: What does CN III supply, and its palsy features?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Most extraocular muscles (all except LR & SO), levator palpebrae superioris, and the pupil (parasympathetic); palsy → a “down & out” eye, ptosis & a dilated pupil.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: What does the trigeminal nerve supply?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Sensation to the face (V1/V2/V3) and motor to the muscles of mastication (V3).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Summarise the four functions of the facial nerve (VII).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Motor to facial expression + stapedius; taste (anterior ⅔ tongue); parasympathetic to lacrimal, submandibular & sublingual glands; and a little general sensation.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: What does CN VIII do, and a classic lesion?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Hearing & balance; a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at the cerebellopontine angle → sensorineural hearing loss (± CN V & VII).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: List the functions of the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Taste & sensation of the posterior ⅓ tongue, stylopharyngeus, parotid (parasympathetic), the carotid sinus/body, and the afferent limb of the gag reflex.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: List the key functions of the vagus nerve (X).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Motor to the pharynx & larynx, parasympathetic to thoraco-abdominal viscera, and the efferent limb of the gag reflex.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: What does the accessory nerve (XI) supply?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: The sternocleidomastoid & trapezius muscles; injury → a drooping shoulder & weak head turning.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which way does the tongue deviate in a hypoglossal (XII) lesion?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Toward the side of the lesion on protrusion (“the tongue points to the lesion”).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which way does the uvula deviate in a vagus (X) lesion?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Away from the side of the lesion (pulled toward the normal side).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Give the afferent and efferent limbs of the pupillary light, corneal and gag reflexes.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Light: II in, III out; corneal: V1 in, VII out; gag: IX in, X out.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: Which cranial nerves are affected in cavernous sinus syndrome?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: III, IV, V1, V2 & VI (plus the internal carotid artery).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: What is jugular foramen (Vernet's) syndrome?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: A lesion of CN IX, X & XI at the jugular foramen (e.g. a glomus tumour) → dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of gag & SCM/trapezius weakness.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.front: What is bulbar palsy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.back: Lower motor neuron lesions of the lower cranial nerves (IX, X, XII) → dysphagia, dysarthria, a wasted, fasciculating tongue and absent gag.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Where does the right and left common carotid artery each arise?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk; the left arises directly from the aortic arch.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: At what level does the common carotid bifurcate, and into what?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: At ~C4 (the upper border of the thyroid cartilage), into the internal & external carotid arteries.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What sits at the carotid bifurcation, and their functions?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The carotid sinus (a baroreceptor, via CN IX) and the carotid body (a chemoreceptor for O₂/CO₂/pH).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What is distinctive about the internal carotid artery in the neck?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: It has NO branches in the neck; it enters the carotid canal and supplies the brain (anterior circulation).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What are the main branches of the internal carotid artery?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The ophthalmic artery, then it ends as the anterior & middle cerebral arteries (of the circle of Willis).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Name the eight branches of the external carotid artery (SALFOPMS).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: Superior thyroid, Ascending pharyngeal, Lingual, Facial, Occipital, Posterior auricular, Maxillary & Superficial temporal (“Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students”).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What are the two TERMINAL branches of the external carotid artery?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The maxillary and the superficial temporal arteries.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Which external carotid branch gives the middle meningeal artery?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The maxillary artery — the middle meningeal is the vessel torn in an extradural haematoma.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Which artery supplies the palatine tonsil?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery (from the external carotid).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Describe the course of the vertebral artery.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: A branch of the subclavian; it ascends through the foramina transversaria (C6→C1), crosses the suboccipital triangle & foramen magnum, and unites with its fellow as the basilar artery.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What circulation does the vertebral–basilar system supply?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The posterior circulation of the brain (brainstem, cerebellum, occipital lobes).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Name the branches of the first part of the subclavian artery.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The vertebral, internal thoracic & thyrocervical trunk.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What is the circle of Willis?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: An arterial anastomotic ring at the base of the brain linking the two internal carotids (anterior) and the basilar artery (posterior) via the anterior & posterior communicating arteries.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What is the internal jugular vein a continuation of, and where does it start?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The sigmoid sinus, exiting the skull through the jugular foramen; it runs in the carotid sheath.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: List the main tributaries of the internal jugular vein.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The facial, lingual, pharyngeal & superior/middle thyroid veins.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Into what does the internal jugular vein drain?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: It joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Describe the external jugular vein.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: Formed by the posterior auricular vein + the posterior division of the retromandibular vein; it crosses sternocleidomastoid superficially and drains into the subclavian vein.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Why is the facial vein clinically important?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: It is valveless and connects to the cavernous sinus (via the ophthalmic veins) — so danger-triangle infection can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Which nodes form the superficial ring of cervical lymph nodes?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: The submental, submandibular, parotid, mastoid & occipital nodes — draining the face & scalp.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Where does all head & neck lymph ultimately funnel?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: Into the deep cervical chain (along the internal jugular vein), then the jugular lymph trunk.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What is the jugulodigastric node, and when does it enlarge?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: A deep cervical node (the “tonsillar node”) below the angle of the mandible; it enlarges in tonsillitis/pharyngitis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What is the jugulo-omohyoid node associated with?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: It is the “tongue node” — lymph from the tongue drains here (relevant in tongue cancer).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: How are the cervical lymph nodes surgically classified?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: As levels I–VI: I submental/submandibular; II–IV upper/mid/lower deep cervical; V posterior triangle; VI anterior/central compartment.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Where does head & neck lymph ultimately drain into the venous system?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: Into the thoracic duct (left) or the right lymphatic duct (right) at the root of the neck (venous angle).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What is carotid endarterectomy used for?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: Removing atherosclerotic plaque from a stenosed carotid bifurcation to reduce the risk of TIA/stroke (a bruit may be heard).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What are the features of temporal arteritis (GCA)?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: A tender, thickened, pulseless superficial temporal artery, headache, jaw claudication & risk of blindness — treat urgently with steroids.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: What is Virchow's node (Troisier's sign)?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: An enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node, classically from gastric cancer spreading via the thoracic duct.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.front: Where is the internal jugular vein relative to the common carotid for central line placement?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.back: Lateral to the common carotid artery (within the carotid sheath, deep to sternocleidomastoid).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient cannot wrinkle the forehead on the affected side and cannot close the eye. This indicates:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Forehead involvement indicates an LMN facial (CN VII) palsy (e.g. Bell's); an UMN lesion spares the forehead because the upper face has bilateral cortical input.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: A midline neck lump that rises on tongue protrusion is a:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: A thyroglossal cyst is tethered to the foramen caecum, so it moves up on tongue protrusion (and swallowing); thyroid masses move on swallowing only.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: A lateral neck cyst at the anterior border of the upper sternocleidomastoid in a young adult is most likely a:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: A branchial cyst (2nd branchial cleft remnant) presents at the anterior border of the upper third of sternocleidomastoid, typically in young adults.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: During thyroidectomy, injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve causes:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the intrinsic laryngeal muscles; unilateral injury causes hoarseness, and bilateral injury can obstruct the airway.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, at risk near the superior thyroid artery, supplies which muscle?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid; injury weakens voice pitch (the inability to sing high notes).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: Perioral tingling and a positive Trousseau's sign after thyroid surgery indicate damage to the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Inadvertent parathyroid removal/devascularisation causes hypocalcaemia — perioral tingling, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs and tetany.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: Which cranial nerve passes THROUGH the parotid gland (and is at risk in parotid surgery)?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The facial nerve (VII) runs through the parotid, dividing it into lobes; a parotid tumour or surgery can therefore cause facial palsy. Secretomotor supply, however, is from CN IX.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: The commonest site of salivary gland calculi is the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The submandibular gland (via Wharton's duct) is the commonest site of stones because its saliva is more viscous and its duct runs against gravity; stones cause mealtime swelling.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: An emergency surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy) is made through the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: A cricothyroidotomy is performed through the cricothyroid membrane between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages — superficial and relatively avascular.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: The 'dangerous area' of the scalp, through which infection can reach the cranial venous sinuses, is the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The loose areolar layer allows infection to spread and reach the intracranial venous sinuses via emissary veins, risking meningitis/sinus thrombosis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: An extradural haematoma is classically caused by rupture of the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Extradural haematoma results from middle meningeal artery rupture, usually with a skull fracture at the pterion; a lucid interval then deterioration is classic (biconvex on CT).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: A subdural haematoma results from rupture of the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Subdural haematoma is due to torn bridging veins (common in the elderly and alcoholics); it appears as a crescent-shaped collection.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: The pterion is clinically important because it is thin bone overlying the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The pterion (junction of frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones) is the thinnest part of the skull and overlies the middle meningeal artery.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: A 'down and out' eye with ptosis and a fixed dilated pupil indicates a palsy of cranial nerve:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: A CN III (oculomotor) palsy gives a 'down and out' eye, ptosis and, if compressive (aneurysm/herniation), a fixed dilated pupil.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis together constitute:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) results from interruption of the sympathetic supply to the head — e.g. a Pancoast tumour or carotid dissection.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: Which structure runs WITHIN the cavernous sinus alongside cranial nerve VI?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The internal carotid artery and CN VI run within the cavernous sinus; CN III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in its lateral wall.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: The common carotid artery bifurcates at approximately which level?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The common carotid bifurcates at about C4 (upper border of the thyroid cartilage) into the internal and external carotid arteries; the carotid sinus and body lie here.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.question: The carotid body, located at the carotid bifurcation, functions as a:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor (sensing O₂, CO₂ and pH); the carotid sinus is the baroreceptor (both signalling via CN IX).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The neurocranium is composed of how many bones?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The neurocranium (braincase) has 8 bones: frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid; the facial skeleton (viscerocranium) has 14.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The pterion is clinically important because it is thin bone overlying the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The pterion (junction of frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones) is the thinnest part of the skull and overlies the middle meningeal artery.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The anterior fontanelle normally closes by approximately:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The anterior fontanelle closes at ~18 months; the posterior fontanelle closes much earlier, at ~2–3 months.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The cribriform plate transmits which cranial nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid, in the anterior cranial fossa, transmits the olfactory nerve (CN I).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve and which vessel?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The optic canal transmits CN II and the ophthalmic artery (a branch of the internal carotid).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: Which cranial nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The superior orbital fissure transmits the ocular motor nerves (III, IV, VI) plus the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal (V1) and ophthalmic veins.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) exits the skull through the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: V2 passes through the foramen rotundum; V3 (mandibular) passes through the foramen ovale ('Rotundum = 2, Ovale = 3').

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The foramen ovale transmits which nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3); the foramen rotundum transmits V2.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The foramen spinosum transmits which vessel?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery (and the meningeal branch of V3).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The internal acoustic meatus transmits which cranial nerves?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The internal acoustic meatus transmits the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves and the labyrinthine artery.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: Cranial nerves IX, X and XI, together with the internal jugular vein, pass through the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI along with the internal jugular vein and sigmoid sinus.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the skull through the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: CN XII passes through its own hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The facial nerve exits the skull through the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The facial nerve enters the internal acoustic meatus but EXITS the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: The inferior alveolar nerve, anaesthetised in a dental block, enters the mandible via the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen on the inner surface of the ramus; it exits at the mental foramen as the mental nerve.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: In an anterior TMJ dislocation, the mandibular condyle moves:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The condyle slips anterior to the articular tubercle (e.g. a wide yawn) and cannot slide back, locking the mouth open.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: An orbital 'blowout' fracture classically traps which muscle, causing diplopia on upgaze?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: A blowout fracture of the orbital floor can trap the inferior rectus (and orbital fat), tethering the eye and causing diplopia on attempted upgaze.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: Periorbital bruising ('raccoon eyes') and CSF rhinorrhoea suggest a fracture of the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: Raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea and haemotympanum are signs of a base-of-skull fracture.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.question: Which structure occupies the sella turcica of the middle cranial fossa?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology.explanation: The pituitary gland sits in the sella turcica (hypophyseal fossa) of the sphenoid, within the middle cranial fossa.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: The muscles of facial expression are all supplied by which cranial nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The muscles of facial expression derive from the 2nd pharyngeal arch and are all supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: Buccinator, which keeps food between the teeth, is a muscle of:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: Despite its deep position, buccinator is a muscle of facial expression supplied by CN VII, not a muscle of mastication.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: The facial nerve exits the skull through the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The facial nerve enters the internal acoustic meatus but exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen, then enters the parotid.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: Within which gland does the facial nerve divide into its five terminal branches?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The facial nerve passes through the parotid gland (dividing it into lobes) and gives its five terminal branches there.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by which branch of the facial nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: General sensation to the skin of the face is provided by the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (V1, V2, V3) provides general sensation to the face; the facial nerve is mainly motor to the facial muscles.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: The cheek and upper lip are supplied by which division of the trigeminal nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: V2 (maxillary) supplies the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip and side of the nose; V1 supplies the forehead and V3 the lower lip/chin/jaw.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: The skin over the angle of the jaw is supplied by the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3), not by V3 — so it is spared in a trigeminal lesion.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: Which layer of the scalp is the 'dangerous area' through which infection can reach the cranial venous sinuses?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The loose areolar layer allows infection/blood to spread and reach the intracranial venous sinuses via emissary veins.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: Scalp lacerations bleed profusely because the arteries:
options: Are held open by the dense connective tissue and anastomose freely
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The scalp arteries lie in the dense connective-tissue layer, which holds them open (they cannot retract), and they anastomose freely across the midline.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: The posterior scalp is supplied sensorially by which nerves?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The posterior scalp is supplied by cervical nerves (greater occipital C2, lesser occipital C2–C3, third occipital C3); the anterior scalp is trigeminal.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: The facial artery pulse is best felt where the artery crosses the:
options: Inferior border of the mandible at the anterior masseter
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The facial artery pulse is felt where it crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the anterior border of masseter.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: Infection in the facial 'danger triangle' can spread to the cavernous sinus because the facial vein:
options: Drains into the external jugular only
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The valveless facial vein connects (via the ophthalmic veins and pterygoid plexus) to the cavernous sinus, so infection can seed cavernous sinus thrombosis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: A patient with a lower motor neuron facial palsy will characteristically:
options: Be unable to wrinkle the forehead on the affected side
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: An LMN (Bell's) facial palsy weakens the whole ipsilateral face including the forehead; an UMN lesion spares the forehead.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: The afferent limb of the corneal (blink) reflex is carried by:
options: The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal (V1)
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The corneal reflex has a V1 (nasociliary) afferent limb and a CN VII efferent limb (orbicularis oculi).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: Vesicles on the tip of the nose in herpes zoster ophthalmicus (Hutchinson's sign) indicate involvement of the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: Hutchinson's sign (nose-tip vesicles) indicates nasociliary (V1) involvement, warning of potential corneal/ocular disease.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: Which of the following is an intracranial branch of the facial nerve supplying the lacrimal gland?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The greater petrosal nerve carries parasympathetic fibres (relaying in the pterygopalatine ganglion) to the lacrimal and nasal glands.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.question: The muscles of MASTICATION (contrasting with facial expression) are supplied by:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Musc.explanation: The muscles of mastication (1st pharyngeal arch) are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal (V3); the muscles of facial expression (2nd arch) are CN VII.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: Which layer of deep cervical fascia splits to enclose sternocleidomastoid and trapezius?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The investing (superficial) layer of deep cervical fascia surrounds the whole neck and splits to enclose SCM and trapezius (and the parotid and submandibular glands).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: The pretracheal fascia encloses which structures?
options: The vertebral column and deep muscles
The thyroid gland, trachea and oesophagus
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid, trachea and oesophagus (and the strap muscles); the prevertebral fascia wraps the vertebral column.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: Sternocleidomastoid divides the neck into the anterior and:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: SCM divides the lateral neck into the anterior triangle (in front of it) and the posterior triangle (behind it).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: Which nerve, running superficially in the posterior triangle, is at risk during lymph-node biopsy?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the posterior triangle superficially and is easily injured in lymph-node biopsy, causing trapezius weakness and a drooping shoulder.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: The 3rd part of which artery is found in the posterior triangle?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The 3rd part of the subclavian artery lies in the posterior triangle, along with the brachial plexus trunks.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: Sternocleidomastoid, acting unilaterally, produces:
options: Face rotation to the same side
Head tilt to the same side and face rotation to the opposite side
Head tilt to the opposite side and face rotation to the same side
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: Unilateral SCM contraction tilts the head to the same (ipsilateral) side and rotates the face to the opposite (contralateral) side.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: The infrahyoid strap muscles are mostly supplied by the ansa cervicalis, EXCEPT the ____ (supplied by C1 alone).
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: Thyrohyoid (and geniohyoid) are supplied by C1 fibres travelling with the hypoglossal nerve, not the ansa cervicalis; the other strap muscles are ansa cervicalis (C1–C3).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: The cervical plexus is formed from the anterior rami of:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The cervical plexus is formed from the anterior rami of C1–C4, lying deep to sternocleidomastoid.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: The cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge at Erb's point, located at the:
options: Anterior border of SCM near the mandible
Middle of the posterior border of SCM
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The cutaneous branches (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, supraclavicular) emerge at the nerve point (Erb's point), the midpoint of the posterior border of SCM.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: The phrenic nerve arises from which roots?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4 and C5 ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive') and provides the sole motor supply to the diaphragm.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: The carotid sheath contains the carotid artery, the vagus nerve and the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The carotid sheath contains the common/internal carotid artery (medial), the internal jugular vein (lateral) and the vagus nerve (posterior, between them).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: Within the carotid sheath, the vagus nerve lies:
options: Posterior, between the artery and vein
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The vagus nerve lies posteriorly within the carotid sheath, in the groove between the carotid artery (medial) and the internal jugular vein (lateral).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: The subclavian artery is divided into three parts by which muscle?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The subclavian artery is divided into three parts relative to scalenus anterior: 1st medial, 2nd posterior, 3rd lateral to the muscle.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: The thoracic duct drains into the venous system at the root of the neck on which side?
options: It drains in the thorax only
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The thoracic duct arches over on the left to drain into the left venous angle (junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: Ludwig's angina is an infection of which space?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: Ludwig's angina is a cellulitis of the submandibular and floor-of-mouth space (often odontogenic) that can rapidly obstruct the airway.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: A retropharyngeal abscess is dangerous because it can spread to the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: Infection in the retropharyngeal space can track down the fascial 'danger space' into the mediastinum, causing mediastinitis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: Compression of the lower brachial plexus and subclavian artery by a cervical rib occurs in the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The interscalene triangle (between scalenus anterior and medius) transmits the brachial plexus trunks and subclavian artery; a cervical rib here causes thoracic outlet syndrome.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.question: Central venous access in the neck is usually obtained via the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Neck.explanation: The internal jugular vein (within the carotid sheath, lateral to the carotid) is the usual site for central venous access in the neck.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: The muscles of the tongue are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve, EXCEPT which one?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: Palatoglossus is supplied by the vagus (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus; all other tongue muscles are supplied by CN XII.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: General sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: General sensation of the anterior two-thirds is via the lingual nerve (V3); taste to this region is via the chorda tympani (VII).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: Taste from the anterior two-thirds travels via the chorda tympani (a branch of CN VII); general sensation is via the lingual nerve (V3).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: The posterior third of the tongue receives both taste and general sensation from the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies both general sensation and taste to the posterior third of the tongue.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: In a hypoglossal nerve palsy, on protrusion the tongue deviates:
options: Toward the side of the lesion
It cannot be protruded at all
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: The tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion because the paralysed genioglossus cannot protrude that side ('points to the lesion').

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: All the muscles of the pharynx are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X) EXCEPT:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: Stylopharyngeus is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); the rest are vagus (X) via the pharyngeal plexus.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: A pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) herniates through:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: A pharyngeal pouch herniates through Killian's dehiscence, a weak area between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx are all supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve EXCEPT the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: Cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: Which is the only muscle that ABDUCTS (opens) the vocal cords?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor of the vocal cords — essential for keeping the airway open.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: Sensation ABOVE the vocal cords is supplied by the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve (from the superior laryngeal) supplies sensation above the vocal cords; the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies below.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: The three auditory ossicles, in order from the tympanic membrane, are:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: From the tympanic membrane inward: malleus → incus → stapes (which sits in the oval window).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: The Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube connects the middle ear to the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx, equalising pressure across the tympanic membrane.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: Young children are prone to otitis media because their Eustachian tube is:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: The child's Eustachian tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal, allowing nasopharyngeal infection to ascend easily to the middle ear.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: Which cranial nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (CN VI); the superior oblique by CN IV; all other extraocular muscles by CN III ('LR6 SO4 rest 3').

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: The superior oblique muscle is supplied by which cranial nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: The superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV); it depresses and intorts the adducted eye.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: A 'down and out' eye with ptosis and a dilated pupil indicates a palsy of cranial nerve:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: A CN III (oculomotor) palsy gives a 'down and out' eye (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique), ptosis and, if compressive, a dilated pupil.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: The afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex is carried by which cranial nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: The afferent limb of the light reflex is the optic nerve (CN II); the efferent limb is the oculomotor nerve (CN III, parasympathetic).
