anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.question: A patient develops horizontal diplopia and the affected eye fails to abduct. Which nerve is palsied?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Special Regions.explanation: Failure of abduction with horizontal diplopia indicates a CN VI (abducens) palsy affecting the lateral rectus.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: Which set of cranial nerves is PURELY SENSORY?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: CN I (olfactory), II (optic) and VIII (vestibulocochlear) are purely sensory; the mnemonic 'Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most' encodes S/M/B.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: Which four cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: CN III, VII, IX and X carry parasympathetic fibres, relaying in the ciliary, pterygopalatine/submandibular, otic ganglia and the visceral walls respectively.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: The trochlear nerve (IV) is unique because it:
options: Is the only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem and decussates
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: CN IV is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the dorsal (posterior) surface of the brainstem and it decussates, supplying the contralateral superior oblique.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: Which cranial nerves pass through the jugular foramen?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X) and accessory (XI) nerves, along with the internal jugular vein.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: The facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves both pass through the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: CN VII and VIII enter the internal acoustic meatus; the facial nerve then continues through the facial canal to exit at the stylomastoid foramen.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: The abducens nerve (VI) is a 'false localising sign' in raised ICP because it:
options: Has a long course angled over the petrous apex, so is easily stretched
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: CN VI has a long intracranial course with a sharp bend over the petrous apex (Dorello's canal), so raised intracranial pressure stretches it, causing a palsy that does not localise the lesion.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: A 'down and out' eye with ptosis and a dilated pupil indicates a palsy of:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: CN III palsy gives a 'down and out' eye (unopposed LR and SO), ptosis (levator palpebrae) and a dilated pupil (parasympathetic loss).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: The motor supply to the muscles of mastication is via which nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: The mandibular division of the trigeminal (V3) supplies the muscles of mastication; the facial nerve (VII) supplies the muscles of facial expression.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: The afferent and efferent limbs of the gag reflex are, respectively:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: The gag reflex has a glossopharyngeal (IX) afferent limb and a vagus (X) efferent limb.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: The afferent limb of the corneal (blink) reflex is:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: The corneal reflex has a V1 (ophthalmic) afferent limb and a CN VII efferent limb (orbicularis oculi).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: In a hypoglossal (XII) nerve lesion, the protruded tongue deviates:
options: Toward the side of the lesion
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: The tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion because the paralysed genioglossus cannot protrude that side ('points to the lesion').

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: In a unilateral vagus (X) lesion, the uvula deviates:
options: Away from the lesion (toward the normal side)
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: With a vagal lesion the soft palate on the affected side is weak, so the uvula is pulled away from the lesion toward the normal side.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: Cavernous sinus syndrome characteristically involves cranial nerves:
options: III, IV, V1, V2 and VI
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: The cavernous sinus transmits CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI (plus the internal carotid), so a lesion there affects these nerves.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: An acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) primarily affects which cranial nerve, and where?
options: CN X, at the jugular foramen
CN II, at the optic chiasm
CN V, at the trigeminal ganglion
CN VIII, at the cerebellopontine angle
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: A vestibular schwannoma arises on CN VIII at the cerebellopontine angle, causing sensorineural hearing loss (and later CN V and VII involvement).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: The cranial nerve nuclei in the MIDBRAIN are:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: The oculomotor (III) and trochlear (IV) nuclei lie in the midbrain; V–VIII are pontine and IX, X, XII are medullary.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: Which cranial nerve provides the sole motor supply to sternocleidomastoid and trapezius?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; injury causes a drooping shoulder and weak head turning.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: Which cranial nerve carries taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue and the afferent gag reflex?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) carries taste/sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, innervates stylopharyngeus and the carotid sinus/body, and forms the afferent limb of the gag reflex.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.question: Bulbar palsy is a lower motor neuron lesion of which cranial nerves?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–X.explanation: Bulbar palsy is an LMN lesion of the lower cranial nerves (IX, X, XII), producing dysphagia, dysarthria and a wasted, fasciculating tongue.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The LEFT common carotid artery arises from the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The left common carotid arises directly from the aortic arch; the right common carotid arises from the brachiocephalic trunk.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The common carotid artery bifurcates at approximately which level?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The common carotid bifurcates at about C4 (upper border of the thyroid cartilage) into the internal and external carotid arteries.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: Which artery has NO branches in the neck?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The internal carotid artery gives no branches in the neck; it enters the carotid canal and supplies the brain. The external carotid supplies the neck, face and scalp.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: Which of the following is a branch of the external carotid artery?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The facial artery is one of the eight external carotid branches (SALFOPMS); the ophthalmic and cerebral arteries arise from the internal carotid, and the vertebral from the subclavian.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The two terminal branches of the external carotid artery are the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The external carotid ends as the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries within the parotid gland.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The middle meningeal artery (torn in extradural haematoma) is a branch of the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The middle meningeal artery arises from the maxillary artery (a terminal branch of the external carotid) and passes through the foramen spinosum.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The vertebral artery is a branch of the ____ and forms the ____.
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The vertebral artery arises from the subclavian, ascends the foramina transversaria (C6–C1) and unites with its fellow to form the basilar artery (posterior circulation).

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The internal jugular vein is the continuation of the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The internal jugular vein is the continuation of the sigmoid sinus, exiting the skull through the jugular foramen and running in the carotid sheath.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: For central venous access, the internal jugular vein lies in what relation to the common carotid artery?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the common carotid artery within the carotid sheath, the basis for its use in central venous access.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The external jugular vein drains into the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The external jugular vein crosses sternocleidomastoid superficially and drains into the subclavian vein.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: All lymph from the head and neck ultimately drains through which nodes?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: All head and neck lymph funnels into the deep cervical chain along the internal jugular vein, then the jugular lymph trunk.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The jugulodigastric node enlarges characteristically in:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The jugulodigastric node (below the angle of the mandible) is the 'tonsillar node' and enlarges in tonsillitis and pharyngitis.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: Cervical lymph nodes are surgically classified into how many levels?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The cervical nodes are mapped as levels I–VI (submental/submandibular, upper/mid/lower deep cervical, posterior triangle, and anterior/central) for cancer staging.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: An enlarged LEFT supraclavicular node from gastric cancer (via the thoracic duct) is called:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: Virchow's node — a palpable left supraclavicular node (Troisier's sign) — reflects metastatic gastric (or other abdominal) cancer draining via the thoracic duct.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: A tender, pulseless, thickened superficial temporal artery with headache and jaw claudication suggests:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: Temporal (giant cell) arteritis affects the superficial temporal artery, causing a tender/pulseless vessel, headache and jaw claudication, with a risk of blindness — treat urgently with steroids.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The carotid sinus, a baroreceptor at the carotid bifurcation, signals via which cranial nerve?
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The carotid sinus baroreceptor is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); the carotid body chemoreceptor is also supplied by IX.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The internal carotid artery's first major branch is the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The ophthalmic artery is the first major branch of the internal carotid, arising after it exits the cavernous sinus; the ICA gives no branches in the neck.

anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.question: The palatine tonsil's main blood supply is the tonsillar branch of the:
anatomy__HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphati.explanation: The palatine tonsil is supplied chiefly by the tonsillar branch of the facial artery (a source of bleeding in quinsy/tonsillectomy).
